title: The sḏm=f of Weak Verbs
short: Weak and irregular verbs change in the sḏm=f: jr=f "he does", dj=f "he gives", mꜣꜣ=f "he sees".
trouble: Students miss jr=f because the j and r are written with one sign, the eye.

blocks.html: Strong verbs look the same in every sḏm=f. Weak and irregular verbs do not (Verb Classes, The Irregular Verbs). Here are the forms you will meet most.

In the sḏm=f, third-weak verbs usually drop the j: jr=f "he does", mr=f "he loves"; some forms double the second consonant instead, jrr=f. rdj usually appears as dj=f "he gives". Doubled verbs show mꜣꜣ=f "he sees" or, in some forms, mꜣ=f.

These changes come from speech. The weak j and the r of rdj faded when vowels moved around them, and scribes wrote what they heard. The doubled forms (jrr=f, mꜣꜣ=f) belong to a group of sḏm=f forms that Gardiner called imperfective; the shorter ones (jr=f, mꜣ=f) to the perfective. You do not need the theory to read: you need to know that jr, jrr, dj and mꜣ are forms of jrj, rdj and mꜣꜣ.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: jr=f "he does": one sign, the eye, writes both consonants of the stem.

blocks.title: Find the verb
blocks.q: gm=f z: what is the verb, and what does the phrase mean?
steps: gm plus a lost weak j: gmj "find".
=f is the subject, z "the man" the object.

blocks.title: One sign, two consonants
blocks.q: Read jr=f mꜣꜥt from the signs: eye, horned viper, then the word mꜣꜥt.
steps: mꜣꜥt "what is right, Maat" is the object.

blocks.html: When you look up one of these forms, undo the change: put back the weak j (mr → mrj), the r of rdj (dj → rdj), or the second consonant of a doubled verb (mꜣ → mꜣꜣ). A doubled second consonant in a third-weak verb (jrr, mrr) is part of the form, not of the root, so take it off as well. The dictionary form is always the full root.

Missing jr=f because the j and r are written with one sign. Students look for a reed leaf j and a mouth r and find only an eye. The eye is a two-consonant sign (More Biliterals) that writes jr by itself. Check: an eye at the head of a clause, followed by a suffix, is almost always a form of jrj "do".
